name: AngelScript
baseline: Duktape (version not stated on the page; July 2015 snapshot). The same table lists PUC Lua at 1.341 s, where AngelScript is slower.
workload: Recursive fibonacci test (tests/fib.*) run as a separate process through the repo's bench tool, wall time including process start-up ('bench 5' in run.bat), July 2015 snapshot; the table value 2.039 s equals the lowest of three logged blocks in bench.csv (2.04581, 2.08138, 2.03945).
claimed_speedup: AngelScript 2.039 s versus Duktape 9.544 s, about 4.7x faster than Duktape (derived from page data); slower than PUC Lua 1.341 s (about 1.5x slower, derived from page data). Scriptorium also lists an AngelScript JIT variant at 1.859 s. In an earlier logged block of bench.csv AngelScript was 2.04581 s versus Lua 2.35924 s and Duktape 14.3008 s.
compiler_and_flags: VS2015 RC where possible, VS2013 elsewhere, linked statically; per-engine flags are not stated in the README (run.bat's plain C reference build uses /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG).
hardware: AMD A10 3.8 GHz (exact model not stated), 8 GiB RAM, Windows 7 64-bit
tradeoffs: Statically typed, C++-like script language with a C++ registration API; the author's own site (angelcode.com) could not be resolved from this environment so its claims were not read. The official GitHub repository is anjo76/angelscript (README: AngelCode Scripting Library, LICENSE.md: zlib-style terms).
caveats: One 2015 recursive-fib test with process start-up counted, run by a third party who writes 'Take it with a grain of salt'; the Duktape version is old and not stated. PUC Lua, Wren, Squirrel, mruby and others in the same table are faster or equal, so the only clear win is over Duktape and the slower tail. Timings vary between logged blocks in bench.csv (Duktape 9.06 s to 14.3 s). A separate April 2026 hobby benchmark (github.com/sashi0034/script-language-benchmark, Windows 10, Visual Studio 17 2022 Release, CPU and units not stated, README says the code was developed mainly with Codex) has AngelScript below Lua on 7 of 16 workloads (float2string 44.533 vs 61.268, mandelbrot 58.432 vs 78.444, native_loop 505.445 vs 506.997, particles_kinematics 933.839 vs 1156.507, queen 253.849 vs 333.410, sha256 321.877 vs 549.956, spectral_norm 188.622 vs 259.634) and above Lua on 9 (for example dictionary 20.888 vs 4.025, sort 328.950 vs 6.175). Prior wave 12 records already hold this repo; this record folds into them.

name: ChakraCore
baseline: QuickJS 2026.06.04 and Duktape 2.99.99 (embeddable JavaScript interpreters in the same CI table); SpiderMonkey jsshell 147.0 and V8 15.7.0 are also in the table
workload: Octane/v8-v7 subset (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run by the repo's CI (commits by 'update-by-ci') with a standalone binary of each engine; the score is a sum over sub-benchmarks, higher is better.
claimed_speedup: Ubuntu section: Score ChakraCore 24767 versus QuickJS 1522 and Duktape 682 (about 16x and 36x, derived from page data). Windows section: ChakraCore 28097 versus QuickJS 1105 and Duktape 371 (about 25x and 76x, derived from page data). Against JIT engines it is not ahead: SpiderMonkey 24412 on ubuntu (about equal) but 18033 on windows (ChakraCore about 1.56x faster, derived), V8 61628 on ubuntu (ChakraCore about 2.5x slower, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Ubuntu build: ahaoboy/ChakraCore-build build.sh clones Microsoft/ChakraCore (--depth=1) and runs ./build.sh, taking out/Release/ch; compiler and flags not stated. The windows section lists version 1.11.24.0, the ubuntu section 1.13.0.0.beta.
hardware: CI runners for the ubuntu, macos-arm64 and windows sections (runner type and CPU model not stated). README result timestamp 10/11/2026.
tradeoffs: JIT engine with a C API; much larger footprint than QuickJS or Duktape (ubuntu listing 19.3M total versus 2.2M for QuickJS and 370.4K for Duktape). The shootout marks macOS arm64 as not supported. README says Microsoft does not intend to support ChakraCore 1.11 after 9 March 2021 and the project continues as a community effort aimed at embedded use cases.
caveats: Third-party shootout regenerated by CI on each run (workflow file not read), so the scores drift (an earlier read of the same README had ChakraCore 19392 versus QuickJS 1217); each engine is run once with no stated variance, runner CPU and compiler flags are not given, and the ubuntu and windows columns run different ChakraCore versions. The comparison against QuickJS and Duktape is JIT versus interpreter, so a large ratio is expected and says little about fairness; the more telling rows are that it ties or beats SpiderMonkey and loses to V8 and Node. Commits are sparse (latest 2026-02-19).

name: Duktape
baseline: MuJS 1.3.8 (embeddable JavaScript interpreter); QuickJS 2026.06.04 is faster than Duktape in the same table
workload: Octane/v8-v7 subset (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run by the repo's CI (commits by 'update-by-ci') with the duk binary; the score is a sum over sub-benchmarks, higher is better.
claimed_speedup: Score Duktape 2.99.99 versus MuJS 1.3.8: ubuntu 682 versus 435 (about 1.57x), macOS arm64 842 versus 522 (about 1.61x), windows (Duktape 2.7.0) 371 versus 339 (about 1.09x), all derived from page data. Binary size on ubuntu: Duktape 370.4K versus QuickJS 2.2M (about 6x smaller, derived from page data). Duktape is slower than QuickJS (ubuntu 682 versus 1522, about 2.2x).
compiler_and_flags: Ubuntu and macOS: ahaoboy/duktape-build build.sh clones svaarala/duktape master and runs make, whose Makefile builds duk with -Os -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-stack-protector -g; windows: release 2.7.0 built with Makefile.cmdline. MuJS build flags were not read.
hardware: CI runners for the ubuntu, macos-arm64 and windows sections (runner type and CPU model not stated). README result timestamp 10/11/2026.
tradeoffs: Footprint-first design (README: portability and compact footprint); ECMAScript 5.1 with selected later features, no JIT. Master is undergoing incompatible changes for Duktape 3.x and 2.x users are pointed to the v2-maintenance branch.
caveats: The project itself does not claim to be faster than any named engine: its docs say footprint matters more than speed and QuickJS is clearly faster (ubuntu 1522 versus 682). The wins recorded here are only over MuJS and weaker engines in a third-party CI shootout (one run per engine, no variance, runner CPU not stated, ubuntu and windows run different Duktape versions, score drifts with every CI run), and the Makefile builds Duktape with -Os, which handicaps speed. The earlier mine-a pass recorded Duktape as no evidence because it read only the project's own pages; this record adds the third-party table. A 2015 Scriptorium run (Windows 7, AMD A10 3.8 GHz, VS2013/2015, recursive fib) has Duktape at 9.544 s versus v7 at 51.940 s (about 5.4x, derived) and Jim Tcl at 12.280 s, but behind PUC Lua at 1.341 s. A JerryScript issue (#4386) peak-memory row (Duktape 582,240 KB versus QuickJS 5,523,792 KB) looks like an aggregate and was not used.

name: CNTK
workload: Keras backend comparison (Keras 2.0.6, cntk 2.0 versus tensorflow-gpu 1.2.1, Theano 0.9.0) on one GTX 1080 Ti: average training seconds per epoch for bidirectional LSTM on IMDb, text-generation LSTM, MLP and CNN on MNIST, FastText on IMDb and CNN on CIFAR-10.
claimed_speedup: GTX 1080 Ti, seconds per epoch, CNTK versus TensorFlow: bidirectional LSTM on IMDb 94.3 versus 245.5 (TensorFlow 2.6x slower per the page); text-generation LSTM 32.7 versus 107.6 (3.3x per the page); MLP on MNIST 1.3 versus 1.9 (1.5x); FastText 2.7 versus 4.5 (1.7x). The page summarises it as CNTK 'about 2 to 4 times' faster than TensorFlow for LSTM. CNTK is slower on CNNs: MNIST CNN 5.0 versus 4.7, CIFAR-10 CNN 24.2 versus 14.2 (TensorFlow about 1.7x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: No compile flags (Python stack): Ubuntu 16.04, CUDA 8.0 + cuDNN 5.1, Keras 2.0.6, tensorflow-gpu 1.2.1, cntk 2.0 (szilard/benchm-dl versions.txt).
hardware: Local machine with a GeForce GTX 1080 Ti Founder's Edition (CPU model not stated); the page also has M60 (Azure NV6), Titan X (Maxwell) and K80 columns, the K80 numbers copied from Max Woolf's blog.
tradeoffs: Deep-learning toolkit with C++ core, Python, C# and BrainScript front ends; the repository was archived by Microsoft on 2026-02-17, the last main release is 2.7 and the README says there are no plans for new features and points users to ONNX and ONNX Runtime. The measured path is the Keras CNTK backend, not native CNTK scripts.
caveats: Third-party 2017-era numbers on old software (TensorFlow 1.2.1, CUDA 8, cuDNN 5.1, CNTK 2.0), one GPU model per column, no variance reported, CPU not stated; the benchmark scripts come from Max Woolf's keras-cntk-benchmark (MIT) but the page does not say that all columns used them. The win is confined to LSTM/RNN and small dense models; TensorFlow is faster on both CNN tests, and the Keras layer may favour either backend. The HKBU dlbench study (arXiv 1608.07249, claims 5-10x over Torch and TensorFlow on CPU LSTMs) was seen only as a search snippet because arxiv.org and dlbench.comp.hkbu.edu.hk are blocked here, so its numbers are not recorded; the hclhkbu/dlbench repo README (MIT, 170 stars) has the harness but no results. The record carries CNTK's own README, which makes no speed claim.

name: Djinni (Snapchat fork of dropbox/djinni)
baseline: original dropbox/djinni generated JNI string conversion (Java to C++ string passing); the README names no baseline explicitly
workload: Passing strings between Java and C++ through Djinni-generated JNI glue; the README's 'Modifications' list gives one line and no benchmark, string sizes, device or version.
claimed_speedup: 'Speed up string passing between Java and C++ (about 5-10x faster depending on string size)'.
stars_or_usage: 238 stars (Snapchat/djinni); dropbox/djinni has 2.9k stars and is archived
tradeoffs: Cross-language binding generator (C++ with Java/JNI, Objective-C and WASM/TypeScript), not a scripting engine. The fork switched the build from sbt/gyp to Bazel, added array<>, outcome<>, future<> and protocol generation, and removed CppProxy finalizers. The djinni.xlcpp.dev documentation site named in the lead belongs to the separate cross-language-cpp djinni-generator and support-lib, whose README has no performance claim.
caveats: First-party one-line claim with no baseline version, string sizes, device, code or method. A search snippet of Snap's engineering post (eng.snap.com, blocked here) says a 16 KB string took more than 2 ms through the original handwritten UTF-8 conversion on a fairly fast device; not verified. dropbox/djinni itself (archived 2020-03-26) makes no performance claim at all, so the original project has no evidence; only the fork's string-passing change does. The 'array<> is an order of magnitude faster than list<>' line compares two Djinni types, not another tool.
